body.text: Srijan Shukla, “Recontextualising Industrial Policy: Lessons from the East Asian Developmental State,” ORF Issue Brief No. 894, Observer Research Foundation, September 2026.

As the post-Second World War order recedes, the political and economic assumptions and certainties that policymakers across the world relied on have considerably weakened. A 2026 report by Global Trade Alert notes that the ongoing Middle East conflict has resulted in over 500 government actions and policy interventions worldwide.[1] From consumer-friendly subsidies and import quotas to export barriers and austerity measures, governments everywhere are deploying all the policy tools at their disposal to mitigate the effects of the Strait of Hormuz crisis. Amid this frenzy, it is easy to miss some important shifts in the underlying economic policy thinking.

During the summer of 2026, two developments signalled a structural shift in industrial policy and the emergence of a new set of assumptions in the post-postwar era. The first was a new World Bank report that provided a comprehensive guide to deploying industrial policy for development in the twenty-first century.[2] The second was the European Union’s (EU) plan to relax the regulations for corporate mergers to facilitate EU-based “global champions.”[3]

These developments mark a watershed moment in mainstream development economics orthodoxy. For decades, institutions like the World Bank and the International Monetary Fund (IMF) advocated for neoclassical economic thinking, as espoused in the Washington Consensus, as the only plausible way out of poverty.[4] This institutional view comes against the backdrop of a long-standing debate between different factions of the economic development academia over the true sources of rapid growth and industrialisation in East Asia.[5]

On one side were economists such as Anne Krueger, Jagdish Bhagwati, and Bela Balassa, who argued that neoclassical economic policies—such as macroeconomic stability, high savings, export orientation, and quality human capital—helped unlock rapid East Asian growth.[6] On the other were supporters of a developmental state, including economists such as Chalmers Johnson, Alice Amsden, Robert Wade, Peter Evans, and Ha-Joon Chang, who believed that a specific set of export-oriented industrial policies were instrumental.[7] Both schools of thought denounced import substitution as practised in countries like Brazil and India as an effective industrialisation strategy.[8]

Institutions like the World Bank and the IMF not only supported the neoclassical faction but actively released literature to refute the role of industrial policy or the developmental state in the rise of the Asian tigers.[9] Moreover, when it came to advising stressed economies, these institutions, especially the IMF, propagated market- and open-trade-friendly, privatisation-centric, and fiscally conservative policies.

These key global organisations are now gradually shifting their stance, marking a pivotal point—after more than half a century of being relegated to heterodox corners, industrial policy is gaining centre stage.

Former US National Security Adviser Jake Sullivan said in 2026, “The most important institutional voice in development economics [the World Bank] just admitted that much of what we thought we knew about what made countries prosper was wrong.”[10]

For decades, especially after the end of the Bretton Woods fixed-exchange rate system in 1971, the US had championed neoclassical policies, espousing privatisation, trade liberalisation, fiscal prudence, a floating exchange rate, and an open capital account. During the Biden administration, of which Sullivan was part, the US pivoted towards industrial policy through the Inflation Reduction Act and the CHIPS and Science Act (2022).[a],[11]

Ironically, the US’s own rise to economic prosperity was achieved through a completely different set of policy choices.[12] However, by the end of the 1980s, the neoliberal consensus had triumphed in the US economy as well and gradually emerged as its overarching framework.[13] The thrust was to avoid any competitiveness-enhancing state support for industries, reflecting rather a determined commitment to maintain a marginal role of the state in the economic sphere.[14] This marked the beginning of the neoliberal era, where fiscal policy took a backseat and macroeconomic management was outsourced to short-term interest rates by central banks.[15]

Currently, the US and leading Bretton Woods institutions, as well as many other nations, have changed their mind on industrial policy. This is not so much because of academic consensus than as a function of geopolitical compulsions. For many governments, from Australia and India to Germany, industrial policy increasingly feels like the only plausible solution to overcome China’s industrial dominance.

The paradox here is that this proliferation is based on a highly reductive conception of industrial policy, a poor caricature of its original iteration as seen in Asia. Successful Asian industrial policy cases were underpinned by certain political economy trade-offs and bargains. For instance, a common bargain would be a dramatic rise in a country’s share of exports to gross domestic product (GDP), but at the cost of mass financial repression, even outright labour subjugation. The Chinese developmental state is built on such compromises. Moreover, each success story had a unique historical process.

Contemporary debates regarding industrial policy essentially ignore these underlying political economy considerations. While the scale of the threat that several countries face from surging Chinese exports and its ever-expanding industrial overcapacity is high, a reductive, decontextualised conception of industrial policy might not be the magic pill most countries hope for. A politically sensitive package of pro-industry incentives, for instance, is unlikely to resolve the profound challenges posed by China’s rise.

This brief outlines the pitfalls of this form of industrial policy. The first section highlights how the China question is changing industrial choices across the developing and the developed worlds. The following two sections outline the core characteristics of industrial policy in East Asia and the historical experience that shaped it in China. The concluding section discusses a necessary reimagining of the idea of industrial policy for it to have any meaningful relevance in this era.

The World Bank and the IMF’s shifting stance on industrial policy as a viable pathway to growth and middle-income status will have profound, long-term implications for the developing world and on global lending politics.[16] For lower- and lower-middle-income countries, a reconfiguration of the global developmental consensus will arguably impact developmental outcomes and eventually result in a rethink of the IMF’s one-size-fits-all structural adjustment programmes.[17] It could potentially compel the IMF to reconsider its long-standing tendency to force painful fiscal austerity upon countries such as Greece and Argentina as a condition for funding.

However, the rising usage of industrial policy, or some version of it, across the developed world, is even more striking. For instance, the EU’s decision to change its mergers-and-acquisitions regulations signifies a strong rupture. While this shift will be celebrated by large European corporations as well as Wall Street’s investment bankers, who will see a rapid surge in dealmaking across the pond, from Brussels’s perspective, it will introduce more competition, which will force companies to innovate more and become more globally competitive. The creation of big national champions is a central feature of classical industrial policy. If the intended outcomes are achieved, it will lead to more globally competitive European firms, but at the cost of declining internal competition. Thus, the EU’s shifting loyalty has an underlying assumption that if industrial policy worked in Asia, especially in China, it will work for EU nations too.

There seems to be a growing impetus in Europe to double down on industrial policy in order to curb rising Chinese imports. The EU had previously hiked tariffs on Chinese electric vehicle imports to create a more level playing field for its domestic manufacturers. Meanwhile, the upcoming Industrial Accelerator Act—the bloc’s most comprehensive attempt at industrial policy—is already irking the Chinese.[18] The Act, if passed, will bar Chinese firms from accessing European public procurement tenders and restrict their ability to take over European firms. The Chinese government has expressed its displeasure towards these moves by cancelling some high-level diplomatic meetings with the EU.[19]

Europe isn’t alone in this pivot. From the 2018 trade war with China to the 2022 CHIPS and Science Act to the 2025 ‘Liberation Day’ global tariffs, the US has attempted to impose some form of industrial policy for several years.[b] Meanwhile, South Korea has its K-Semiconductor Belt strategy, the UK has deployed green industrial subsidies, and Thailand has adopted a 30@30 electric vehicle transition policy.[20] From former poster children of neoliberalism to modern architects of industrial policy, almost everyone has jumped on the industrial policy bandwagon.

However, this spread of industrial policy suffers from conceptual confusion. It belies the very idea of what industrial policy aims to achieve, and more operationally, resolve. As economic commentator Noah Smith observed, industrial policy “has become too broad of a category,” which makes it harder to have a constructive discussion around it.[21] He said, “Most people think of it [industrial policy] as government promotion of specific industries—autos, or electronics, or maybe just manufacturing in general. Others see export promotion—which is more about where products are sold than about which products they are—as the key industrial policy. Some people see FDI [foreign direct investment] promotion as industrial policy; others don’t.”

The unspoken part here is that for first- and third-world nations, China seems to be the illness and the cure of their industrial troubles and larger political economy predicament.[22] The first ‘China Shock’ deindustrialised the US, especially regions that faced direct import competition. [c],[23] While its scale is fiercely debated among trade and labour economists, manufacturing as a share of GDP dropped from 16 percent in 1997 to 11 percent in 2021.[24]

Now, China Shock 2.0 is wreaking economic havoc across Europe and Southeast Asia, and ensuring that there is no level playing field for the rest of the world.[25],[26] As a report in Foreign Affairs states, “China’s economic gravity is suffocating the very economies it has promised to lift. Trade deficits with Beijing have ballooned as local industries, from textile producers in Indonesia to steel makers in Thailand, struggle against a flood of underpriced Chinese goods.”[27]

The modern Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) economic model has been built on maintaining complex supply chains with Chinese firms, which cumulatively produce most of the globally consumed goods. Over the past decade, while Southeast Asia’s contribution to global manufacturing value-added has remained at 5 percent, China has seen its share rise from 18 to 28 percent since 2012.[28]

While the surging Chinese exports, which resulted in a trillion-dollar surplus in 2025, are battering global markets, China’s underlying industrial model is the most attractive solution for policymakers.[29] The sheer scale of Chinese industrial policy,[30] especially after the country’s real estate bust,[31] has attracted global attention, pushing policymakers to invest in their own industrial policies. Their objective is to incentivise more domestic manufacturing, or more realistically, stop the bleeding caused by cheaper Chinese imports.

The obsession with Chinese exports seems to be deluding governments into thinking of industrial policy as a ‘magic pill.’ Consider the two key industrial objectives of Western capitals these days: supply-chain resilience and rebuilding a domestic manufacturing base. However, these are two separate goals, often requiring contradictory policies.[32] While one objective aims to limit the risk of weaponised (inter?)dependence, the other seeks to revitalise advanced industrial societies that have fallen prey to social decay and the rise of radical politics in the aftermath of deindustrialisation.

Industrial policy, as conceptualised in postwar Asia, was designed to achieve neither of those outcomes. This conceptual muddle is resulting in the decontextualisation of how industrial policy worked in some Asian countries—there is hardly any emphasis on the sociopolitical bargains and institutional arrangements that underpinned successful industrial-policy cases in Japan, South Korea, Taiwan, China, and even India.

Chinese thinker Wang Hui, speaking to economic historian Adam Tooze, observed, “Our present has a double face. Perhaps we should think of a ‘return’ not simply as a repetition, but rather as something new that emerges from the attempt to recreate something old.” [33] The same applies to the West’s attempts at industrial policy. In an effort to recreate the half-century-old economic miracles of East Asia, the rest of the world will end up creating something altogether different, most of which would neither be successful nor productive.

There is also an active effort to rid the Asian industrial policy experience of its political economy baggage; history is being reinvented to suit present-day narratives. According to this version of industrial policy, introducing a set of incentives for some specific sectors, coupled with some trade barriers for those industries, is all that governments need to do to facilitate rapid manufacturing development.
Some of the actual key characteristics of the modern industrial policy playbook, as observed in postwar East Asia, are given in the next paragraphs.[34]
First, the prime objective is to facilitate catch-up growth via industrialisation.[35] Asian countries were relatively lower-income nations and needed a pathway to higher growth.

Second, to achieve manufacturing capabilities, a few industries were selected for preferential treatment.[36] Sometimes referred to as ‘steering,’ this act of picking one sector over others is a central aspect of industrial policy that goes against the core philosophy of neoclassical thinking.
Third, industrial policy is inherently export-oriented and this preferential support is conditional on a sector’s export performance.[37]

Fourth, pursuing such a policy paradigm requires the state to address a series of market failures by coordinating between domestic industry, labour, capital, export markets, and the government.[38] In most cases, this involves some degree of labour subjugation. Another common feature is a certain degree of financial repression, which effectively directs savings away from households and towards industry.

Fifth, these coordinating mechanisms require a de facto autonomous bureaucracy, referred to by sociologist Peter Evans as embedded autonomy.[39] This bureaucracy can seek feedback from the industry and discipline it when necessary, resulting in dynamic policymaking.

The aforementioned factors should be seen more as a spectrum than a rigid set of conditions for industrial policy. No two countries have identical successful industrial policies.[40] They are contingent on specific historical contexts and aim to resolve individual market failures. Industrial policies are inherently dynamic and require constant reconfiguration and institutional arrangements that can undertake such dynamic policymaking.

China’s breakneck economic rise over the past half-century presents one of the most bewildering case studies.[41] However, attributing its entire manufacturing success to the ‘black box’ of industrial policy—which the state magically pivoted to during the Deng Xiaoping Era—is empirically inaccurate. In stark contrast, China underwent a series of developments over the course of the twentieth century that ultimately resulted in a unique polity. This particular polity, with all its distinctive features, implemented a version of industrial policy that suited its ‘state design.’

Chinese intellectual Wang Hui in The End of the Revolution: China and the Limits of Modernity provides an incisive overview of how the Chinese experience through the end of the Qing Dynasty, the Kuomintang Era, the Maoist regime, and the early Deng Era, gave the federal state a distinctive identity.[42] He shows how Mao’s insistence on pursuing a distinct Communist-revolutionary nation-building project, separate from the Soviet Union, gave China a unique form of political independence, which in turn shaped its sovereign character. Similarly, some of the disastrous policy experiments under Mao, such as the Great Leap Forward and the Cultural Revolution, led to a state that was willing to allow constant self-experimentation.[43] During the Cultural Revolution, Mao famously sent central government officials down to the villages and townships, which allowed them a vital grassroots-level understanding of the republic.[44] Similarly, the constant peasant mobilisation fundamentally altered social dynamics between the state and labour.

It is necessary to step back further in time to make sense of the modern Chinese developmental state. As Italian economist and sociologist Giovanni Arrighi points out in Adam Smith in Beijing: Lineages of the Twenty-First Century, China had a remarkably well-developed national market in the eighteenth century itself,[45] arguably more complex and mature than any other domestic market. Yet, as Hui argues, a series of steps was required to transform this national market into today’s world-beating industrial behemoth.[46]

As he writes, “Through national efforts during the late Qing (Dynasty) to construct a modern military and commercial system, as well as the Agrarian Revolution that continued after the Xinhai Revolution (1911), a new form of internal-external relations was created that differed from that under the traditional national market. In discussing the state character of Modern China, it is impossible to leave aside the transformation in land relations and rural identities that occurred as a result of Chinese revolution.”

In operational terms, as defined by economist Yingyi Qian, the Mao-era federal decentralisation provided the bedrock for the federal decentralisation during Deng’s reform era. [47] Today, this delegation of “real authority” to local governments is credited with providing the first manufacturing push through the 1980s via township and village enterprises (TVEs). All these features of China’s federal design eventually culminated in a unique type of state formation and allowed China to implement its successful industrial policies.

This analysis is not an attempt to whitewash the excesses of the Chinese state through the decades; rather it simply illustrates how industrial policies are not divorced from a country’s historical experience. On the contrary, they are a solution to the challenges a country’s social, political, and economic history throws up. Therefore, to think of industrial policy as a global template is the antithesis of its original conception.

Scholars have argued that all countries that industrialised following the Industrial Revolution featured some degree of industrial policy.[48] For instance, Ha-Joon Chang shows how a mix of infant industry doctrine and trade protectionism helped the US become a manufacturing behemoth through the second half of the nineteenth century.[49] The story was similar for countries across the Atlantic.

Paul Bairoch’s data on industrial tariffs from 1870–1913 challenges the idea that free trade drove Western industrialisation.[50] Apart from countries such as the UK and the Netherlands, most major economies, including the US, France, Russia, and Italy, relied heavily on protectionism, with the US maintaining tariffs of 40–50 percent throughout much of the period. Meanwhile, many of the countries practising freer trade were European colonies, where trade policy largely served imperial rather than domestic interests.

Going ahead, any discussion about how countries can leverage industrial policy should begin by fundamentally reinterpreting the concept according to their current predicament. While no two industrial policies are alike, they share a threefold common thread: all industrial policies are export-oriented, meant to facilitate catch-up growth, and aspire to resolve country-specific market failures. The real question is which of these features is applicable to specific economies, such as Germany, India, France, or Brazil.

While all countries can export and need to resolve market failures, catch-up growth is primarily a developing world concern. A flailing German automobile and high-technology machinery sector, for example, could arguably use some industrial policy assistance to become competitive again.[51] However, a country like the US that deploys industrial policy to diversify away from China’s rare earth magnets might reduce its reliance on the latter but is unlikely to unlock meaningful export incomes given existing Chinese overcapacity in these sectors.

The first step towards adopting an industrial policy should be to identify what such a strategy aims to accomplish. Defining the aim will decide if a country even needs industrial policy or not. A government needs to identify distinct objectives, such as supply-chain resilience versus re-industrialisation versus facilitating industrialisation in a lower-income economy to undertake structural transformation.

More concretely, on the one hand, in countries like Japan and South Korea, the need for supply-chain resilience stems from China’s weaponisation of certain products and critical inputs, as well as recurring geopolitical shocks. On the other, for countries in Southeast Asia or Europe, protecting existing industrial hubs against Chinese import competition is a distinct objective from supply-chain resilience. Meanwhile for lower-middle-income countries like India and Bangladesh, industrial policy is an attempt to develop a robust manufacturing sector that can rapidly create jobs and growth. Entirely distinct from these cases are post-industrial countries such as the US and the UK, where the purpose of reindustrialisation is to correct domestic political economy imbalances, especially in a highly financialised economy dominated by low-wage service jobs.[52]

It is unlikely that industrial policy will yield meaningful results in all of these cases. It will arguably work better for industrial countries facing import competition. If the aim is supply-chain resilience in sectors with existing global overcapacity, the underlying industries might require state support for a prolonged period. However, industrial policy is unlikely to help a country like the US fundamentally reindustrialise. It can allow the US to build advanced semiconductor facilities, but it is doubtful that any labour-intensive sectors like textile or shoe-manufacturing can be brought back. American wages are too high for some of these low-cost manufacturing sectors to survive. Moreover, the advanced chip facilities will result in some job creation, but nothing on the scale necessary to fundamentally alter the average American’s reliance on low-paying service jobs. Ideally, the US needs more efficient and targeted welfare policies to mitigate some of the country’s inequality, not industrial policy.

Finally, what ultimately determines the success or failure of an industrial policy is whether its design takes into account a country’s specific bureaucratic, social, and political characteristics. Two distinct cases from India’s developmental experience help illustrate how and when an industrial policy actually works.

India launched its own version of industrial policy through its Production Linked Incentives (PLI) scheme in 2020. While it has seen some success, such as in electronics manufacturing, the absence of an embedded bureaucracy has hurt its prospects across most targeted sectors.[53] Yet, throughout the late 1970s to the early ’90s, the Indian government—part intentionally and part inadvertently—made a series of policy interventions amounting to an industrial policy that resulted in the rise of India’s highly export-oriented information technology (IT) sector.[54] In this case, the state implemented policies to address specific coordination problems and market failures in a partial-command economy setting, rather than acting on some abstract conception.

To make industrial policy work, one has to first define the objectives. The second step is recognising the local state capacity constraints and the nature of bureaucratic and industry incentives at play. Finally, an industrial policy should be crafted that either works regardless of underlying political economy challenges, or is designed to alleviate them.

Intelligent state intervention, especially that which can leverage the power of markets, is undeniably a powerful instrument. Unlike import substitution, the discipline imposed by export markets makes industrial policy an efficient framework.

In the current geopolitical climate, industrial policy appears all the more attractive as a reasonable response to China’s daunting manufacturing capacity and the resulting deindustrialisation in many countries. For the rest of the world, the impulse to undertake an industrial policy is understandable, but insufficient by itself, primarily because the scale of Chinese industrial policy and overcapacity is large enough to drown out minor efforts elsewhere. Thus, countries that genuinely wish to pursue industrial policy at this juncture must begin by reconsidering the contours of their relationship with China, especially when it comes to trade. In turn, this will shape the scope and design of the painful domestic bargains required to sustain such a strategy. For instance, some trade barriers against China will result in a fall in Chinese imports, but is likely to result in higher short-term inflation. Nations will have to accept some of these painful trade-offs. They might also have to coordinate their strategies with other like-minded countries to create a response large enough to mitigate some of the global macroeconomic effects resulting from Chinese overcapacity.

A good industrial policy is one that understands what it aims to achieve, addresses local complexities, has the capacity to adapt and evolve, and most importantly, is willing to accept some painful trade-offs.

[a] While the Inflation Reduction Act specifically targeted green industries, such as solar and electric vehicles, the Chips Act aimed to turn the US into a semiconductor manufacturing hub. Collectively, they signalled the emergence of an explicit American attempt at industrial policy.

[b] On April 2, 2025, the US government under President Trump imposed sizeable tariffs on several countries, coupled with a baseline 10 percent duty on all its trading nations. President Trump referred to April 2 as Liberation Day. Over time, the US negotiated deals with most countries, bringing down individual country-level tariffs. However, the average weighted tariff for the US currently stands at 11.1 percent, which is much higher than the 2.4 percent on the eve of Liberation Day.

[c] In the years following China’s admission into the World Trade Organization (WTO) in 2001, there was a massive surge in cheap Chinese exports to several countries in North America and Europe. This led to large-scale deindustrialisation of existing industrial hubs and towns, especially in countries like the US and the UK. This wholesale destruction of industrialised clusters, for instance, in Northern England and the Rust Belt in the US, has been referred to as “China Shock.” The term itself originates from academic papers by David Autor, David Dorn, and Gordon Hanson (2013-16), which showed the impact of the labour market and social conditions on American towns facing intense import competition from China.
